newsitem.title: UK: Opposition Labour poised to win key UK byelection.
newsitem.headline: Opposition Labour poised to win key UK byelection.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party looks poised to win a key parliamentary by-election on Thursday, snatching a seat from the ruling Conservatives and setting what it hopes will be the pattern for a looming general election.

The loss of the prosperous northwestern English constituency of Wirral South would put the ruling Conservatives into a minority in parliament and make it more difficult for Prime Minister John Major to cling to power

Major must hold a general election within the next three months and political analysts believe the Wirral South poll will be an important guide to whether his party stands any chance of winning an unprecedented fifth term in office.
Opinion polls suggest it cannot. They have consistently given the Labour Party led by Tony Blair a lead of around 20 percentage points.
A poll in Thursday's Times newspaper put Labour 21 points ahead of the Conservatives, down four from a month ago.

But the opinion pollsters were proved wrong at the 1992 general election and Major's party has taken comfort from the fact that it has always won back at a general election seats it lost in by-elections.

By-elections are widely seen as an opportunity for voters to register their dissatisfaction with the government's performance. At general elections, large numbers of voters remain loyal to the parties they elected before.

"There are a lot of people who see by-elections as an opportunity to kick the government. We would expect to see that," Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine said shortly after the by-election was announced.
But this case may be different. There has never been a by-election so close to a general election and neither Labour nor the Conservatives have left anything to chance.
For the past three weeks, senior figures from both parties have been pacing the streets of Wirral South, knocking on doors, sweet-talking voters and kissing babies.
The Conservatives easily won Wirral South at the 1992 general election with more than 50 percent of the vote. They have held the seat since it was created in 1983.
But when Heseltine himself visited the constituency this week, he got a hostile reception.
"You've ruined our health service," one old aged pensioner told him after he complimented her on the daffodil in her buttonhole.
On the eve of the poll, Labour's shadow foreign secretary Robin Cook was in the constituency, brimming with confidence.

"The voice of Wirral this week will echo across Britain. It will be a blast that will bring down a tottering Tory (Conservative) government and will bring in a Labour government that looks to the future, not the past," Cook told a party rally.
